transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-17
Time: 20:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai
Attendees: Liam Ortega (Redwood AE), Asha Patel (Redwood SE), Daniel Ruiz (CTO, Ember), Priya Kapoor (Lead Backend), Oliver Green (DevOps)

Summary:
Quick SDK walkthrough focused on environment bootstrapping and auth patterns for Ember Analytics' early pilot. SE showed Python and TypeScript quickstarts, talked through API keys vs service accounts, env var patterns, KMS considerations, and Redwood Console settings for orgs. Customer raised data residency, SOC2, and dedicated capacity questions. Agreed next steps: starter repo, security pack, and a dedicated scoping call for Private/Dedicated options.

Topics covered:
- Quickstart: python + typescript examples and minimal auth setup
- Local dev to CI/CD pattern, env vars, and secret management (KMS/HSM)
- Service accounts vs user API keys; rotating keys and audit logs
- Console walkthrough: routes, cost breakdown, model pinning, and rollouts
- Redwood Optimize suggestions: batching, caching, quantization guidance for Ember workloads
- Enterprise constraints: SOC2, SSO/SAML, VPC/private control plane, data residency

[00:00] Liam: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick intro — I'm Liam, I'm the AE for this account, and Asha from our solutions team will do the SDK walkthrough. Daniel, Priya, Oliver, you all good on time?
[00:12] Daniel: Yep all good. thanks.
[00:14] Priya: good to go.
[00:16] Asha: Hi, nice to meet you all. I'll share my screen in a sec — showing the repo and console. Apologies if the names get a little noisy in the transcript.
[00:24] Oliver: No worries. We're most interested in the auth patterns and how you'd recommend integrating with our CI/CD. we run Jenkins + GitHub Actions for quick jobs.
[00:32] Asha: Perfect, I'll hit both local dev and CI patterns. I'll start with the Python quickstart — then TypeScript.

[02:05] Asha: (screen) Ok here is the repo: /quickstarts/sdk-starter. On the python side we have requirements: redwood==1.3.0 (example), requests, and a tiny helper wrapper. To initialize, you export REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var locally and use the Redwood client:
- from redwood import RedwoodClient
- client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))

[02:37] Asha: For Typscript we show dotenv and the official @redwood-ai/client (note: package name in this demo is illustrative). The pattern: set REDWOOD_API_KEY in CI secrets. For long-lived workloads we recommend service accounts — we'll explain.

[04:10] Priya: service accounts — do you have a recommended lifecycle? rotate keys how often? and do you support short-lived tokens?
[04:22] Asha: Great Q. We support both long-lived API keys (scoped) and short-lived tokens via our service-account flow. Best practice: create a service account per environment, scope permissions to only generation/embeddings endpoints needed, and rotate keys quarterly or on deploy. For extra security, you can use short-lived tokens minted by your own auth layer and exchange them with Redwood's token endpoint. We'll include an example in the starter repo.

[05:30] Daniel: Do you have an example with KMS? We want to avoid plaintext keys in CI logs.
[05:38] Asha: Yes. In the repo we have a snippet using AWS KMS + Secrets Manager and a sample GitHub Actions step. Basically store encrypted secret in Secrets Manager, decrypt in a limited runner step, and inject into process env only for the job. Also note Redwood can integrate with customer KMS for Private deployments if you need HSM-backed keys.

[06:50] Oliver: For Private, we'd probably need the control plane inside our VPC. Is that what you do?
[06:59] Liam: Short answer yes — Private offers a customer-managed control plane option and we can run the inference runtime in your VPC or on-prem. Asha will discuss seeding and config in the scoping call; we'll schedule that.

[08:15] Asha: Back to code. Demo: simple generation request in Python — we show streaming vs non-streaming. Example call: response = client.generate(model='redwood-llama-3b', prompt=..., stream=True). We'll show how to wire up streaming to a websocket consumer in TS.

[09:40] Asha: On the Console side (quick tour) — we've got org settings, API keys view, routes, and model catalog. You can pin models to routes, set canary rollouts, and configure automatic fallback to smaller quantized variants when capacity is low. Also cost breakdown per route (token-level) so you can see what features cost.

[11:05] Priya: How accurate is the cost breakdown? Our finance team will want line-item forecasting.
[11:14] Asha: The Console projects per-token cost, and you can attach custom overrides for quantization profiles. For pilots we can produce a conservative estimate using your token distribution. We'll run a tracer with 1000 sample requests if you can share typical prompts.

[12:25] Daniel: OK — can Redwood Optimize give us suggestions tailored to our prompts? For example whether to use batching or a smaller model for reranking?
[12:36] Asha: Yes — Redwood Optimize (opt... sometimes mis-says as "optimize toolkit") analyzes workload profiles. It will suggest batching configs, cache prefixes for repeated prompts, and where quantization will keep quality. We'll include an Optimize report sample with the starter repo.

[14:02] Oliver: About latency. Our product needs p95 sub-250ms for short prompts. How likely is that on hosted vs dedicated?
[14:14] Liam: Hosted might get you close for small models in nearby regions, but Dedicated reserved pools give much tighter p95 SLOs. We can target p95 <200ms with reserved capacity on A100/H100 depending on model and sequence length. There's always a tradeoff: Dedicated higher baseline cost, hosted cheaper but variable under load.

[16:00] Priya: If we start with hosted during pilot and then move to dedicated, how are rollouts handled?
[16:10] Asha: That's part of our deployment abstraction: same API and route config. You pin route to a model version, then change routing policy to use Dedicated nodes for production. Canary and A/B rollouts are in Console. You can also set automatic fallback to hosted variants.

[17:25] (small crosstalk)
[17:48] Asha: I'm going to walk through the TypeScript quickstart now. Example: import {Redwood} from '@redwood-ai/client'; const client = new Redwood({apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY}); // use fetch streaming polyfill for Node 18+

[19:10] Asha: For local dev we give a .env.development and .env.test. Important pattern: don't check .env.production into repo; use templates like .env.example and populate secrets via CI secrets or vault. We'll include a sample config for deploying to Kubernetes with a secretRef and an init container that fetches secrets from a vault.

[20:45] Oliver: On the infra side, what network egress patterns should we expect if using hosted? Outbound to Redwood endpoints, right? Any IP allowlists?
[20:56] Asha: Yes hosted expects outbound to our API endpoints. We publish a set of IP ranges for enterprise customers and can support allowlist for Dedicated endpoints. For Private we don't need outbound at all — you control the network. We will share the IP range docs but will confirm exact CIDR blocks in the scoping call.

[22:10] Daniel: Security: SOC2, ISO, SSO — can you briefly outline what you have and what you provide to customers?
[22:22] Liam: We have SOC 2 Type II, ISO-27001 in progress, SSO via SAML/SCIM provisioning, RBAC in Console, audit logs for tokens and admin actions. We'll send the security kit after the call.

[23:45] Priya: For audit logs, are token accesses tied to user ids? We need per-call attribution for compliance.
[23:56] Asha: Yes — if you use short-lived tokens minted from your SSO, we can attribute calls to the service account or user id in logs. The Console shows request-level logs with token id, route, model, and latency.

[25:30] Daniel: Can you show an example of the CI step for GitHub Actions?
[25:38] Asha: (screen) Yes: step: - name: fetch secrets uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials ... run: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id ember/redwood/apiKey --query SecretString --output text) - name: run tests run: REDWOOD_API_KEY=$REDWOOD_API_KEY npm test. We also have a pattern that wraps the key in a short-lived ephemeral token for tests to ensure it doesn't live in logs.

[27:12] Oliver: Do we have to use aws? We're multi-cloud — GCP secret manager + KMS would be better for us.
[27:22] Asha: Totally fine. The starter repo has examples for AWS, GCP, and Azure KeyVault. For KMS-wrapped keys on Private deployments we can plug your KMS so customer never sends plaintext to Redwood.

[29:00] (brief pause while Asha navigates files)

[30:15] Asha: A couple of gotchas: 1) watch out for token leak in logs (mask before printing); 2) streaming requires proper client-side backpressure; 3) batching can increase latency for single-shot requests if misconfigured. We'll include a checklist.

[31:22] Priya: About batching — our workloads are mix of short chat messages and large analysis prompts. Will Optimize recommend per-route batching configs?
[31:34] Asha: Yes per-route. You can set different policies for the chat route (low batch latency, smaller batch sizes) and analysis route (batch aggressively). Optimize gives per-route latency vs cost curves.

[33:00] Daniel: Any concerns about PII? we'll likely process user messages. retention?
[33:12] Liam: Hosted defaults to ephemeral logs for user payloads, retention configurable. We have data retention controls and can disable logging for specific routes. For regulated data you should consider Private deployment. We'll include data retention knobs doc.

[34:50] Oliver: Sizing question: for pilot we plan 3 models: small for embedding/rerank, medium for chat, and a larger one for heavy analysis. Any quick rule of thumb costwise per 100k tokens?
[35:05] Asha: Rough back-of-envelope: small ~ $X / 100k tokens, medium ~ $Y / 100k, large more — we'll produce a precise estimate once you share token distribution. Liam will follow up with a sample cost sheet based on typical prompt length and token counts.

[36:20] (laughter)
[36:45] Asha: I'm going to demonstrate a tiny end-to-end: local dev -> run a sample request against hosted route -> show Console trace for that single request. (shares Console) You can see tokens, model, latency, and cost. We also toggle canary to route a small % to a different model.

[38:10] Priya: About model versioning — if we pin a model and Redwood updates the underlying weights, is there a version hash we reference?
[38:22] Asha: Yes we provide explicit model versions and a version id. You pin to version id and we surface change logs. For major changes we give deprecation notices. You can also snapshot model configs for reproducibility.

[39:50] Daniel: For the starter repo, can you include Ember-specific config: region eu-west-1, smaller timeouts, and a sample nginx ingress config we can copy?
[39:59] Asha: Absolutely — that's an easy add; we'll tailor .env.example and k8s manifests. We'll commit a branch called ember-custom.

[41:05] (short silence)
[41:20] Oliver: If we wanted to run an internal benchmark, do you provide a harness or load-testing scripts?
[41:30] Asha: We have a benchmark harness and workload generator we can share. For Dedicated pilots we can run a joint load-test; SE+DevOps pair to run it. We'll do a smoke bench for p50/p95.

[43:00] Priya: Any compliance weirdness around storing embeddings? We sometimes want to persist them for search and analytics.
[43:10] Liam: Embeddings stored in your infra is the safest; we provide an embeddings output that you can choose not to persist in Redwood. For hosted we can also provide a retention policy. If you need full control, Private deployment is recommended.

[44:25] Asha: Wrapping up the demo: I'll paste the starter repo link in the chat and highlight files to look at: README.md, examples/python/simple_gen.py, examples/ts/stream_demo.ts, ci/github-actions.yml, infra/k8s/secret-ref.yaml, optimize/report-sample.md.

[45:10] (chat: link pasted)

[46:00] Daniel: On pricing, what's the quickest way to get ballpark for trial? we want to propose internal budget.
[46:10] Liam: I'll send a simple pilot pricing sheet for 3 models + example monthly token volumes. If you go Dedicated we'll have a committed capacity quote. Expect the pilot estimate by EOD Friday.

[47:25] Priya: Anything we should watch for in integrating SDK with our backend that breaks discoverability or permissions?
[47:36] Asha: Keep secrets out of logs, scope service account permissions, and use per-service accounts for each microservice. Use route-level permissioning if you want to lock a route to a team. We'll show how to do RBAC with SCIM groups.

[48:50] Oliver: Final — can you run through the next steps so we're all aligned?
[48:58] Liam: Sure. Next steps: 1) Asha: starter repo + ember-custom branch; 2) Liam: SOC2 pack + pilot pricing; 3) schedule Private/Dedicated scoping call week of Sep 29 (Oliver, Asha, Liam); 4) Ember to share a small sample of prompts for Optimize analysis.

[50:10] Daniel: Sounds good. Also I'll share our compliance questionnaire for quick answers on retention.
[50:18] Liam: Perfect. We'll aim to get the repo and docs to you by Sep 18 and the pricing by Sep 19.

[51:00] (meeting close)
[51:05] Asha: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and in the chat with the starter repo. Bye!
[51:10] Daniel: Thanks. Bye.

End of transcript.
